title: Five gates around Makkah
note: The page's five miqat gates around Makkah, one for each direction, each an arrow pointing inward to the House.

lines.text: Five roads into Makkah, one rule for all

lines.text: For Hajj, the nearer begin where they are
Five lines, one for each direction

research.retell: Five fixed boundary lines ring Makkah, one for each direction of travel, and no one heading to Hajj or Umrah may cross theirs without first entering ihram.
proof: Five gates set on a ring around Makkah, one for each direction of arrival, each with an arrow pointing inward to the House.; no one crosses a line without ihram

no one crosses a line without ihram; A miqat is a boundary line in space. The Prophet ﷺ appointed one for the people of each direction, and no person intending Hajj or Umrah may cross his line without being in ihram.
Dhul Hulayfah, for the people of Madinah and anyone coming through it, about four hundred and fifty kilometres out and the furthest of them, known today as Abyar Ali.
Al-Juhfah, for the people of Sham, Egypt and the west, north of Makkah, with Rabigh used in its place today.; the north west
Qarn al-Manazil, for the people of Najd, to the east.; And Dhat Irq, for the people of Iraq, to the north east.
Yalamlam, for the people of Yemen, to the south, used also by many arriving from South and Southeast Asia.

The four schools agree that crossing the miqat without ihram while intending the rites obliges either a return to the line or a sacrifice.; Hanafi hold that if he returns to the miqat and enters ihram there, the sacrifice falls away; the Shafi’is hold similarly, and the difference between them lies in whether the return must be before he begins any rite.
Whoever lives nearer than a miqat enters ihram from where he is, until the people of Makkah enter from Makkah itself.; whoever is nearer begins where he is
one for each direction of arrival; al-ihram, entering the sacred state
